dedupe_keys.name: resilience of ukraine s internet during the full scale war 2022 to 2023

description: This post-event and recovery case follows how Ukraine's internet kept working after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. RIPE NCC analysts used RIPE Atlas probes and BGP data from the Routing Information Service to compare the network on 1 January 2022 with 1 April 2023. They found that the number of Ukrainian autonomous systems fell by 6.2 per cent (1,781 to 1,677), foreign upstream networks by 12 per cent, and domestic interconnections by 5.8 per cent, while internet exchanges such as UA-IX stayed stable, pointing to a strong local peering fabric. Russian upstream networks fell from 48 to 21 and came to serve mainly occupied areas. In Kherson, routes were forced through Russian networks from mid-2022, raising latency and imposing Russian blocking, and reverted to Ukrainian transit after liberation in November 2022; the Kerch Strait bridge explosion in October 2022 added 5 to 10 ms on routes that relied on a cable across it. Other analysts credit many cross-border exit points, well-provisioned transit, local peering, backup channels such as Starlink and operator cooperation; the EU estimated about a quarter of telecom infrastructure damaged by 2023. Coverage: national, 2022 to 2023. Format and access: RIPE Labs articles, Chatham House and Cloudflare analyses, free; the Atlas and RIS data are open. Caveats: measurement coverage thins in occupied and front-line areas. Simulation uses: network resilience under attack, rerouting and recovery of interconnection, and dependence on cross-border links. Related records: RIPE Atlas and RIS data, and the Starlink geomagnetic storm case for satellite backup.
